issues.description: The verbal definition of type diagnosticity gives the wrong denominator. As written, diagnosticity = (words with suffix in category) / (total words in that category), which is P(suffix|category). However, the token definition uses 'all words that contain the suffix' as the denominator (P(category|suffix)), and the reported values confirm the latter: e.g., -IAN diagnosticity 0.54 and -ABLE A/N/V values (0.977/0.023/0.000) sum to 1 across categories, which is only possible if the denominator is the total number of words containing the suffix. The text therefore misdescribes how the central construct was computed, undermining replicability and creating an internal contradiction with the token definition.
issues.quote: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.description: A z-value of 0.60 cannot correspond to p < 0.01 (z = 0.60 implies p ≈ 0.55). Either the reported z or the p-value for the token specificity interaction is incorrect. Because this is one of the key 'graded' analyses used to argue that behaviour mirrors corpus statistics, the error directly affects the central claim.
issues.quote: such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.subcategory: text vs table discrepancy in key statistics
issues.description: The in-text statistics for Experiment 3 do not match Table 5. The text reports go-past B = 41, t = 3.837, but Table 5 lists B = 43, t = 3.76. For regressions-out the text reports B = 0.3, z = 3.12, while Table 5 lists B = 0.25, z = 2.65. These are the two effects on which all of the Experiment 3 conclusions rest, so unexplained discrepancies between the narrative and the table are serious.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01).

issues.description: In Experiments 1 and 2 the mixed models include only a random intercept for subjects, with no random effect for items or suffixes. Because the predictor (suffix condition/diagnosticity/specificity) varies at the suffix/item level and each suffix is repeated across many trials, omitting by-item/by-suffix random effects treats stimuli as fixed and inflates Type I error (effectively pseudoreplication across only ~20 or ~11 suffixes). This is inconsistent with Experiment 3, which does include random intercepts for suffixes, indicating an unjustified analytic inconsistency.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: Experiment 3 tested six eye-movement measures and then probed two of them for diagnosticity interactions, explicitly without a priori predictions about which measures would be affected and without any correction for multiple comparisons. With several measures tested at alpha = .05 and only two reaching significance, the risk of capitalizing on chance is substantial, and the framing ('we chose to monitor a variety') reflects undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.description: The abstract and introduction frame the work as characterizing the relationship between 'spelling and meaning,' but the operationalization is restricted to grammatical lexical category (noun/adjective/verb). Lexical category is a syntactic/grammatical property, not semantic meaning, yet sweeping claims about 'transmission of meaningful information' and 'access to meaning' are built on it. The construct being measured is narrower than the construct being claimed.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of “meaning”).

issues.description: The Conclusion of the computational section states that diagnosticity (spelling-to-meaning) should affect spelling production and specificity (meaning-to-spelling) should affect print-to-meaning tasks. This is the reverse of both the logical feedforward mapping and of what the Experiments section states and what was actually done (diagnosticity used in the print-to-meaning judgement and reading studies; specificity used in the spelling production study). The contradictory statement could confuse interpretation of the predictions.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading).

issues.description: Experiment 1 lost 11.7% of data points to timeouts or non-response button presses under a 2-second deadline, but there is no analysis of whether missingness was related to condition or to suffix diagnosticity. If harder-to-classify (less diagnostic) items timed out more often, the diagnosticity effect could be biased by non-random missingness. The handling of the missing data is also not described (e.g., listwise exclusion).
issues.quote: on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response)

issues.description: In Experiment 3 the number of words before the target differed reliably between congruent and incongruent sentences (4.75 vs 5.23, p < .05). Pre-target sentence length/word count affects launch position, parafoveal preview, and later reading-time/regression measures (go-past, regressions-out), which are precisely the measures showing significant effects. Matching on letters but not on word count leaves a plausible confound for the key effects.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: The entropy analysis is used to claim that spelling carries more lexical-category information than phonology, but the mean entropy difference is trivial (0.61 vs 0.63). The conclusion rests on a regression slope marginally below 1 rather than a direct test of this negligible mean difference, and a 0.02 difference in mean entropy is unlikely to be practically meaningful. The strong conclusion ('generally yield better prediction') overstates the result.
issues.quote: the spellings of derivational suffixes generally yield better prediction of lexical category (mean H=0.61) than do their spoken realisations (mean H=0.63).

issues.description: The paper repeatedly makes a strong functional-causal claim that English spelling 'maximises the transmission of meaningful information,' implying the writing system evolved for this purpose. The supporting evidence is correlational/diachronic description, which cannot establish that spelling-sound inconsistency arose in order to maximize meaning transmission. The teleological framing ('maximises') is not warranted by the data.
issues.quote: We close by arguing that English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.

issues.description: No a priori power analysis, sample-size justification, or pre-registration is reported for any of the three experiments, despite multiple graded analyses, subgroup splits, and the post hoc model-improvement tests. Sample sizes (46, 29, 47 undergraduates) appear convenience-based. The OSF link is data/materials only ('view_only'), not a pre-registration, leaving substantial undisclosed analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: Data for all experiments can be found in the OSF storage for this project.

issues.description: Experiment 1 forces a noun-vs-adjective binary choice and omits verbs entirely, even though the broader claim concerns three lexical categories. This both narrows the construct and can inflate apparent sensitivity (participants must pick one of two options that the stimuli were designed to map onto). Verb diagnosticity is also acknowledged to be weak, so the experiment cannot test the full claimed system.
issues.quote: You will be asked to decide if a letter string looks like a noun or an adjective.

issues.description: The conclusion that morphological cues 'facilitate access to meaning' goes beyond the data, which only show sensitivity to lexical category in artificial nonword tasks. No measure of meaning access (comprehension, semantic judgement) was obtained, so the facilitation-of-meaning claim is an inferential leap from grammatical-category sensitivity.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so (see our spelling and eye tracking data) suggesting that these cues facilitate access to meaning.

issues.description: All participants are Royal Holloway undergraduates reading British English, yet conclusions are framed for 'skilled readers' generally, and the constructs are claimed to 'reflect general cognitive principles' that 'must manifest' in other orthographies. The narrow, homogeneous sample and single language do not support claims about universal cognitive principles or other writing systems.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.subcategory: interaction interpreted despite non-significant simple effects
issues.description: For go-past times the diagnosticity-by-congruency interaction is reported as significant, yet neither simple slope is significant (congruent t = 0.634; incongruent only a 'trend', p = 0.13). Interpreting this as diagnosticity 'modulating' processing is weak when no condition shows a reliable diagnosticity effect, and the model-improvement chi-square (df=2) bundles the main effect with the interaction, making it hard to attribute the improvement to the interaction.
issues.quote: there was no effect of diagnosticity on go-past times in the congruent condition (B = 8.30, t = 0.634, p > 0.5), whereas there was a trend towards an effect in the incongruent condition (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13).

issues.description: Suffixes were selected as 'noun-diagnostic' or 'adjective-diagnostic' using a threshold of diagnosticity >= 0.50, but some included suffixes are essentially ambiguous (e.g., -AN has noun diagnosticity 0.50 and adjective diagnosticity 0.496 per Appendix A). Treating near-balanced suffixes as diagnostic exemplars weakens the manipulation and biases the categorical condition effect toward null while still being labelled diagnostic.
issues.quote: These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50, and occurred in at least 20 different words.

issues.subcategory: claim of two distinct constructs not jointly tested
issues.description: The authors argue that diagnosticity and specificity are distinct and that both are necessary (rather than a single cue-validity measure), but the two constructs are never entered into the same model or tested for incremental predictive value; each is examined in a separate experiment. Given their substantial correlation (r = 0.53), the claim that both are necessary is asserted rather than demonstrated.
issues.quote: Here we hypothesise that the bidirectional relationship between the form and the meaning cannot be captured using a unitary concept (e.g. cue validity), and needs to be expressed through the combination of diagnosticity and specificity (probability of a cue given a category).

issues.description: The graded diagnosticity/specificity effects on behaviour are interpreted as readers tracking corpus statistics, but the behavioural regressions do not control for correlated lexical properties of the suffixes (e.g., type/token frequency, orthographic length, neighbourhood). The authors themselves report diagnosticity correlates with frequency, so the graded behavioural effects could reflect frequency or other distributional covariates rather than diagnosticity per se.
issues.quote: This analysis revealed a main effect of diagnosticity on response type: B = 0.87, z = 4.13, p < 0.0001, such that more diagnostic suffixes were more likely to be ascribed to the category that they denote.

issues.subcategory: overstated specificity claim vs computed value
issues.description: The text repeatedly states that adjectives are 'virtually always spelled –OUS' for the /əs/ sequence, but the authors' own specificity value for -OUS is only 0.81 (Table 3 and Appendix A), i.e. roughly four in five, not 'virtually always.' This overstates the strength of the flagship example used to motivate the constructs.
issues.quote: Berg and Aronoff (2017) observed that given the sound sequence /–əs/, adjectives are virtually always spelled –OUS.

issues.description: Comprehension accuracy is reported as '0.86%' (and a range of 0.66%–0.98%), which is presumably 86% (0.66–0.98 as proportions). As written, the values are uninterpretable and could indicate near-zero comprehension, which would call task engagement into question. The reporting error should be corrected.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.subcategory: mislabeled effects (simple slopes as main effect)
issues.description: In the regressions-out analysis, condition-specific (simple) slopes are described as 'a main effect of diagnosticity' while simultaneously reporting separate values for the congruent and incongruent conditions plus an interaction. Labeling conditional simple effects as a main effect is imprecise and can mislead readers about what was actually estimated.
issues.quote: First, there was a main effect of diagnosticity: the probability of regressing to previous regions of the sentence decreased as diagnosticity increased in the congruent condition (B = -0.15, z = -2.31, p < 0.05), and increased as diagnosticity increased in the incongruent condition (marginal significance, B = 0.21, z = 1.8, p = 0.08).
